features.eyebrow: One collector · one identity chain · dashboard + MCP
features.title: Connect the signals behind an incident.
features.lead: One collector connects traces, logs, product analytics, session replay, LLM observability, and alerts. Engineers follow those links in the dashboard. AI agents can query the same records through evidence bundles, structured references, and MCP tools.

items.title: Distributed tracing
items.body: OTLP-native ingest. Spans, baggage, and propagation work with first-party Node, Go, and Rust SDKs — and any OpenTelemetry SDK over OTLP.

items.title: Structured logs
items.body: JSON logs with severity, automatic trace correlation, and per-module loggers. Auto-attached to the active span — no copy-paste IDs.

items.title: Agent-readable evidence
items.body: Evidence bundles compact repeated logs, rank spans, preserve citations, and return retrieval refs so agents can expand raw logs, profiles, replay, AI calls, or tool calls on demand.

items.title: SDKs and MCP server
items.body: First-party SDKs for TypeScript, Go, and Rust plus an MCP server that lets agents inspect traces, logs, replays, profiles, agent runs, actions, tools, changes, and evals.

items.title: Interaction ID to CPU
items.body: A click mints one interaction_id. Backend spans, logs, AI calls, and action graphs join through the resulting trace. CPU profiles join too when profiling is enabled and samples are indexed by trace ID.

items.title: Session replay
items.body: Browser sessions recorded with rrweb, stored as DOM-mutation chunks in R2, and replayed inline next to the trace they belong to.

items.title: Usage analytics
items.body: Page views, interactions, errors, UTM parameters, and identity stitching — the product-analytics layer, in the same store as your traces.

items.title: AI and agent actions
items.body: LLM calls, retrievals, tool calls, agent runs, eval cases, tokens, USD cost, latency, and failure category — all linked into one causal action graph.

items.title: Alerts
items.body: Alert rules over any signal — latency, error rate, AI spend, custom usage events. One rules engine and one notification surface across the stack.

items.title: User profiles
items.body: Identity linking from anonymous visitor to logged-in user, with traits and event history. Every signal can be filtered by user and replayed from their perspective.

items.title: AutoSRE & change correlation
items.body: Correlate deploys, feature flags, and config changes with traffic-normalized cohort error lift and noisy-neighbor contention checks. Remediation is policy-gated: MCP write tools are opt-in, and your own runner executes any approved change.

ccr.title: Give the agent investigation-ready context, not a telemetry dump.
ccr.lead: CCR means compressed context retrieval: the collector clusters repetitive logs, selects exemplars, ranks failed spans and critical paths, correlates traces/actions/profiles/replay, and hands the agent explicit retrieval refs for deeper inspection. The agent still controls expansion; the platform just makes the first packet useful.
ccr.beforeTitle: Raw-tool debugging makes the agent ask for everything.
ccr.beforeBody: Without CCR, an agent tends to page through broad logs, full traces, profile metadata, replay metadata, and action records separately. Repeated messages like hundreds of identical 404s consume context even though one exemplar plus count is enough to start.
ccr.afterTitle: Evidence bundles summarize first, expand second.
ccr.afterBody: With CCR, the agent asks for one compact bundle anchored on a trace, action, agent run, or tool call. The response includes summaries, evidence refs, compaction records, suggested pivots, and retrieval refs for raw data that remains available but explicit.
ccr.benchmarkTitle: Benchmark by running the same incident twice: CCR off, then CCR on.
ccr.benchmarkLead: Use fixed anchors, the same agent prompt, and the same token budget. In the off run, let the agent use raw tools such as log search and trace detail. In the on run, start with get_evidence_bundle and only expand retrieval refs the agent chooses. Compare token input, tool calls, raw rows read, cited evidence, and whether the same root cause is reached.
ccr.benchmarkResultTitle: Measured CCR run: 500 repeated 404 logs collapsed to 3 exemplars.
ccr.benchmarkResultLead: Local benchmark run on June 4, 2026 against the shipped evidence retrieval route. This uses a separate failure fixture, not the slow-checkout proof: a checkout trace with a failed payment span and 500 correlated 404 log rows. CCR preserved the failed payment span reference while reducing the first context packet.
ccr.benchmarkDocLabel: Read the benchmark methodology and raw output

benchmarkCases.name: Repeated 404 burst
benchmarkCases.withoutCcr: Search logs around the failing trace and return the broad result window.
benchmarkCases.withCcr: Cluster matching log signatures, include exemplars, and attach a logs retrieval ref.
benchmarkCases.measure: Raw log rows read vs. exemplar count, prompt tokens, and whether the answer cites the trace and exemplar log.

benchmarkCases.name: Slow checkout trace
benchmarkCases.withoutCcr: Load the full span tree, then ask the model to infer the critical path.
benchmarkCases.withCcr: Return failed spans, critical path summaries, and connected profile refs up front.
benchmarkCases.measure: Spans included in context, top latency span agreement, and profile ref expansion rate.

benchmarkCases.name: Agent tool regression
benchmarkCases.withoutCcr: Fetch agent runs, actions, tool calls, eval rows, AI calls, traces, and logs separately.
benchmarkCases.withCcr: Anchor on the agent run or tool call and return causal path, side-effecting tool refs, failed evals, and connected traces.
benchmarkCases.measure: Tool calls made by the debugging agent, correct failed tool/eval identification, and evidence citations.

benchmarkCases.name: Replay/profile deep dive
benchmarkCases.withoutCcr: Include replay/profile metadata early even when the agent may not need it.
benchmarkCases.withCcr: Expose replay event-window and profile-frame refs but require explicit expansion.
benchmarkCases.measure: How often agents expand deep refs, payload bytes read, and whether unnecessary raw replay/profile data stays out of context.

architecture.title: One collector. Your telemetry graph.
architecture.lead: Instrumented services write telemetry into Observability Unified. Humans and agents read the same connected graph through dashboard APIs, compact evidence bundles, structured evidence references, and MCP tools, while ingest credentials stay separate from investigation access.
architecture.connectedGraphBody: evidence IDs, compact bundles, traces, logs, replay, AI cost, actions, CPU

faq.a: Observability Unified is a self-hosted observability platform that gives AI agents context to debug production software. One collector connects traces, logs, replay, profiles, and agent activity. AI agents retrieve compact evidence bundles with citations through MCP, and engineers inspect the same records in the dashboard. A local Docker image includes the collector, dashboard, storage, and optional sample data.

faq.q: Can agents investigate incidents in applications that do not use AI?
faq.a: Yes. Agents can use MCP to investigate ordinary production incidents using traces, logs, service maps, replays, and other connected evidence. For applications that use AI agents, the Agent Action Graph also shows runs, model calls, tools, costs, and evals.

faq.q: Can AI agents inspect Observability Unified through MCP?
faq.a: Yes. The Observability Unified MCP server exposes tools for status, traces, logs, service maps, AI sessions, users, replays, connected signals, profiles, evals, agent runs, actions, tool calls, evidence bundles, retrieval refs, evidence expansion stats, recent changes, change blast radius, and similar findings. Remediation tools are registered only when writes are explicitly enabled. Agents can start from a failing trace, AI cost spike, user session, profile frame, analysis result, or action ID and gather the same evidence an engineer sees in the dashboard.

CCR means compressed context retrieval. Instead of sending an agent every correlated log, span, replay chunk, profile frame, AI call, and tool payload immediately, Observability Unified returns a compact evidence bundle first: clustered log exemplars, ranked spans, citations, compaction provenance, suggested pivots, and retrieval refs. The raw evidence remains available, but the agent has to expand it intentionally.

faq.q: How is it different from Datadog, Sentry, or PostHog?
faq.a: Its primary difference is unification for debugging. APM traces, logs, product analytics, session replay, AI observability, alerting, profiles, agent action graphs, and analyses live in one collector and one dashboard, correlated through a single identity chain and exposed to agents through MCP. Many observability vendors now offer MCP servers; see the comparison for sourced details. Here, MCP tools are read-only by default and return compact evidence bundles with citations, evidence references, confidence, exemplar pivots, and retrieval refs that link back to the same records the dashboard shows. It also runs on your own infrastructure, so no external telemetry vendor sits in the data path.

faq.q: What is the Agent Action Graph?
faq.a: The Agent Action Graph shows what an agent did and what each step caused. It links browser actions, agent runs, LLM calls, retrievals, tool calls, guardrails, backend traces, logs, profiles, and eval cases through stable action IDs. Engineers see it in the dashboard; AI agents can traverse the same graph through MCP.

faq.q: How does AutoSRE keep an AI agent from rolling back the wrong deploy?
faq.a: AutoSRE separates link provenance (relationshipCertainty: exact, inferred, heuristic) from causal proof (causalProofTier: unverified_locus, corroborated_candidate, cohort_rate_isolated, counterfactual_verified), and a per-action policy matrix decides what each tier allows. For rollback_deploy and toggle_feature_flag, a stack frame overlapping a changed file only reaches corroborated_candidate, which needs human approval in the dashboard, and unverified_locus is blocked. A grant without human approval needs traffic-normalized cohort error lift (with minimum sample sizes and noisy-neighbor contention checks) or paired baseline-fail/candidate-pass counterfactual eval runs. Config and prompt changes need counterfactual verification. MCP write tools stay unregistered unless you set OBS_MCP_ENABLE_WRITES. The collector only issues a single-use grant; your own runner claims it and executes the change.

Retention is controlled by the RETENTION_HOURS environment variable on the collector and defaults to 72 hours. Profile blobs have a separate PROFILE_RETENTION_HOURS override because they're larger per record. Because everything lives in your storage account, you set the policy and pay the storage directly; there's no per-event retention tier to negotiate.

faq.q: When do I outgrow D1, and what's the upgrade path?
faq.a: D1 is the default low-ops hosted path for small and medium deployments. The practical ceiling depends on event volume, cardinality, and retention, so heavy installs should move to the Node collector with Postgres plus S3-compatible blob storage before D1 becomes the bottleneck.

faq.q: How does it handle PII and GDPR?
faq.a: Self-hosting is the headline answer: data never leaves your infrastructure, so residency and processor questions reduce to where you deploy. On top of that, the usage-event pipeline applies default-redact scrubbing on ingest; fields named like email, token, password, authorization, or cookie are stripped from context and properties JSON before storage. Session replays use rrweb, which masks input fields by default and supports per-element block/mask attributes.

faq.q: Does it support SSO or multi-user dashboards?
faq.a: Not today. Two auth boundaries ship: a write-only ingest API key for SDKs and a single password for the dashboard. Multi-user, RBAC, and SSO are out of scope and tracked separately. Most teams put the dashboard behind their existing identity proxy, such as Cloudflare Access or Tailscale, in the meantime.

faq.q: Can I migrate from Datadog, Sentry, or PostHog?
faq.a: Sentry, PostHog, Honeycomb, and older @obs/* package migrations are covered in the docs. For Datadog, OTLP-native ingest accepts the standard OpenTelemetry SDK over OTLP HTTP, so traces and logs are usually a configuration change; a dedicated walkthrough is tracked separately.

faq.q: Does it work with my existing OpenTelemetry SDK?
faq.a: Yes. The collector accepts OTLP over HTTP using JSON or protobuf, with gzip. gRPC is intentionally not supported because Cloudflare Workers cannot host it, and OTLP HTTP covers every official SDK. The first-party SDKs are thin wrappers that point the standard OpenTelemetry SDK at the collector and add OpenInference helpers for LLM and tool spans.

faq.q: Where can I self-host Observability Unified?
faq.a: Start locally with Docker. For production, choose Cloudflare Workers with D1 and R2, or deploy the Node collector with Postgres and S3-compatible object storage.
